newsitem.title: USA: Democrats approve Romer, unveil fundraising reform.
newsitem.headline: Democrats approve Romer, unveil fundraising reform.

text.p: President Clinton's Democratic Party, facing a damaging investigation of its fundraising practices, installed Colorado Gov. Roy Romer as chairman on Tuesday and announced moves to clean up the mess.

At Clinton's request Romer took over as general chairman and will act as the party's chief public spokesman. Clinton asked Massachusetts businessman Steve Grossman, who is close to Vice President Al Gore, to be national chairman in charge of day-to-day activities at party headquarters.

The new leadership was approved by acclamation at a meeting of the party's national committee, which immediately announced reforms of Democratic fundraising practices. Under these reforms, Democrats will no longer accept donations from non-citizens or U.S.-based subsidiaries of foreign companies and will limit donations to $100,000 per person per year.
"There have been some mistakes that have been made. Our absolute determination is that we're going to ... do everything we can humanly do to avoid those mistakes in the future," Romer told Reuters.

Democrats face a difficult year with Republicans who control Congress eager to pursue revelations that the party illegally raised large sums of campaign money from foreign donors and individuals who could not substantiate the source of the money they gave.
The Justice Department was looking into the matter and Clinton was under the microscope from critics who charged that overseas donors attempted to influence his conduct of U.S. foreign policy.

Romer urged Republicans to join the Democrats in limiting the influence of big money on U.S. politics. "Come join us. We're not trying in any way to make political hay. We honestly need to have the cooperation of both parties," he said.
Democrats had to return more than $1.5 million, much of it raised by fundraiser John Huang, who tapped his contacts with Asian corporations to raise the funds.
Under the new rules Democrats would have raised $6.5 million less in 1996, party officials said.
